title: Practical Biochemistry and Molecular Biology
tagline: Learn the hands-on grammar of the biochemistry lab: measure, separate, copy and cut the molecules you have been reading about.
overview: This is the course where Levels 1 and 2 turn into hands. Over thirteen technique modules you move from the unglamorous foundations (safety, notebooks, buffers, pipetting) through the workhorse measurements of biochemistry (spectrophotometry, protein assays, centrifugation, chromatography, SDS-PAGE and western blotting, enzyme kinetics) into the core molecular-biology toolkit (DNA and RNA extraction, agarose gels, PCR and qPCR, cloning and transformation), and finish with the skill that makes every experiment count: analysing, graphing and reporting data honestly. The modules follow the standard practical content for a BSc Honours biochemistry and molecular biology laboratory course and are organised to complement the parallel lecture courses (Metabolism, Gene Expression, Recombinant DNA Technology). Treat each unit as a pre-lab primer: read it before the session, then use the videos and protocols to rehearse the bench steps in your head.
whyItMatters: Almost every claim in biochemistry rests on a measurement someone made at a bench. If you can prepare a correct buffer, build a reliable standard curve, run a clean gel and keep a notebook another person could repeat, you can work in a research lab, a diagnostic laboratory, a food or pharmaceutical quality unit, or move into a research degree with confidence.
careerLinks: Research assistant or technician in a research institute or laboratory
Quality control and analytical chemist in pharmaceutical, food or beverage industry
Molecular biologist in agricultural or biotechnology research
Graduate research (MPhil/PhD) in biochemistry, molecular biology or biotechnology
studyTips: Read the protocol before the session and write the calculations (volumes, dilutions, expected results) in your notebook beforehand. Most bench mistakes are arithmetic mistakes made in a hurry.
Record what you actually did, not what the manual said. Deviations are data, and they are often the explanation when an experiment surprises you.
After every practical, redraw the key figure by hand (a standard curve, a gel, an amplification plot) and write two sentences on what it shows and what could be wrong with it.
Pair up the techniques: when you meet a gel, ask what was loaded and what extraction, quantification and buffer came before it. Seeing the pipeline end to end makes each unit easier.

units.title: Laboratory Safety, Good Practice and the Lab Notebook
units.hook: A lab notebook is the only witness to what you really did at the bench, and it must still make sense to a stranger, or to you, three years from now. Safety and record keeping look like paperwork, but they are the habits that separate a reproducible result from an anecdote.
learningObjectives: Identify the main hazard classes in a biochemistry lab (chemical, biological, electrical, radiological, physical) and the controls for each.
Read a safety data sheet and choose suitable personal protective equipment and waste stream for a reagent.
Explain why biological material is handled and disposed of according to its biosafety level.
Write a dated, complete notebook entry with aim, method, raw data, observations and conclusions.
Prepare a simple risk assessment for a planned experiment.

keyConcepts.definition: A hazard is something that can cause harm; risk is the chance it will, given how you use it. Risk assessment asks how to lower that chance.
A standard document for each chemical that lists its hazards, safe handling, first aid, spill response and disposal. Not to be confused with sodium dodecyl sulfate, which shares the abbreviation.
Coat, gloves, eye protection and closed footwear: the last line of defence, used after engineering controls (fume hood, safety cabinet) and safe procedures.
A tiered scheme (BSL-1 to BSL-4) matching containment practice to the danger of the organism; most teaching labs work at BSL-1 or BSL-2.
Working so that you neither contaminate the sample with microbes nor release microbes into the room: flame or ethanol, clean surfaces, no talking over open plates.
The original, time-ordered notebook or electronic record of observations. Raw data go here first, not onto loose paper or a phone.
Others (or you later) can repeat the work and get comparable results, which requires lot numbers, volumes, instrument settings and exact conditions to be written down.

deeper.beginner: Before you touch anything, know where the eyewash, shower, fire blanket and exits are. Wear a coat and closed shoes, tie back hair and take gloves off before touching door handles or your phone. Never pipette by mouth and never eat or drink in the lab. In the notebook, write the date, the title and the aim, list what you did in order, paste or tape in raw data, and note anything odd. Use ink, cross out mistakes with a single line and never tear out pages.
deeper.intermediate: Safety is built in layers: eliminate or substitute a hazard first (use a safer reagent), then use engineering controls (fume hood for phenol, chloroform and acrylamide powder; biosafety cabinet for pathogens), then administrative controls (training, signage, procedures) and finally PPE. A risk assessment lists each step, the hazard, who might be harmed, the control, and what to do if it goes wrong. For records, adopt the habit of writing so that the entry is complete the same day: reagent names with supplier and lot, concentrations and volumes, instrument names and settings, filenames of data, and a clear separation between observation (the solution turned pink) and interpretation (so the enzyme is active).
deeper.advanced: Good laboratory practice treats documentation as part of the experiment: traceable reagents and equipment calibration, written standard operating procedures, contemporaneous entries, witnessed and signed records, and controlled changes. Electronic lab notebooks add version history and searchable metadata, but the underlying principles of attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original and accurate data (often abbreviated ALCOA) are the same. Poor documentation is a documented contributor to irreproducible results, and investigators increasingly publish raw data and protocols alongside papers. Thinking about a project's data management (file naming, backups, metadata, analysis scripts) from day one prevents the common fate of unlabelled files named final_v3_REAL.

commonMistakes: Recording data on scraps of paper or a phone camera roll and meaning to copy it up later; the original is what counts.
Writing the method as a copy of the manual rather than what was actually done, hiding real deviations.
Treating gloves as protection from everything: contaminated gloves spread chemicals and DNA, and ordinary gloves are no barrier to some solvents.
Pouring waste down the sink without checking the SDS or the lab's waste stream.

units.title: Solutions, Dilutions, Pipetting and Buffers
units.hook: Nearly every experiment you will ever run begins with a solution someone had to make correctly, and nearly every unexplained failure turns out to start there too. A buffer that is half a pH unit off or a pipette used outside its range can quietly ruin a week of work.
learningObjectives: Calculate the mass or volume needed to prepare a solution of given molarity, percent w/v or percent v/v.
Use C1V1 = C2V2 and serial dilutions to make working solutions and standards.
Select and use an appropriate air-displacement micropipette correctly.
Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation to design a buffer and prepare it by titrating to the right pH.
Explain why buffer pH changes with temperature and concentration and choose a buffer with a suitable pKa.

keyConcepts.definition: Moles of solute per litre of solution. Moles = mass divided by molar mass, so a 0.5 M solution of a 100 g/mol compound needs 50 g per litre of final solution.
A concentrated, stable stock is diluted to the working concentration on the day of use, saving time and reducing weighing errors.
The amount of solute is conserved on dilution: concentration times volume before equals concentration times volume after.
A series of repeated, equal-factor dilutions (for example 1:10 each step) used to span a wide concentration range or to count cells and colonies.
A mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). It predicts the pH of a buffer and tells you what base-to-acid ratio you need.
A buffer works best within about one pH unit either side of its pKa, where both the acid and base forms are present in useful amounts.
A piston-driven pipette that draws liquid with an air cushion; accuracy depends on using tips of the right size, the right pressing technique and the right volume range.

deeper.beginner: To make 100 mL of 0.1 M Tris (molar mass about 121 g/mol), weigh about 1.21 g, dissolve in less than 100 mL of water, adjust the pH, then add water up to the 100 mL mark in a volumetric flask. Always dissolve first and top up to volume last, because the solute itself takes up space. When pipetting, press to the first stop, dip the tip just below the surface, release slowly, then press to the second stop to empty. Use the smallest pipette that covers your volume.
deeper.intermediate: Pick a buffer whose pKa is within a unit of the target pH and that does not interfere with your assay: phosphate can inhibit some kinases and precipitates calcium, Tris reacts with some reagents and has a strongly temperature-dependent pKa (it falls by roughly 0.03 per degree Celsius, so a Tris buffer set to pH 7.5 at room temperature is noticeably more basic on ice and more acidic at 37 degrees Celsius), while HEPES and MOPS are less sensitive. Prepare most buffers by dissolving the weak acid or base form, then titrating with strong acid or base to the desired pH at the temperature of use, rather than mixing calculated amounts of both forms. Calibrate the pH meter with at least two standards that bracket your target and rinse the electrode between samples. Ionic strength matters because the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation uses concentrations, whereas real pKa values depend on activity.
deeper.advanced: Henderson-Hasselbalch assumes ideal behaviour and negligible contribution from water and from extreme dilution; at very low concentrations or near the ends of the pH range, the full charge-balance equation is needed. Buffer capacity is greatest at pH = pKa and is proportional to total buffer concentration, so a 10 mM buffer will be overwhelmed sooner than a 100 mM one, but the higher ionic strength may inhibit your enzyme or alter protein-protein interactions. The Good buffers (HEPES, MES, MOPS and relatives) were designed in the 1960s with pKa values in the physiological range, high water solubility, minimal membrane permeation, low metal binding and little temperature dependence, which is why they are standard in biochemistry. Pipetting error is dominated by operator technique: temperature differences between liquid and pipette, speed, angle, pre-wetting, viscous liquids and volatile solvents all bias delivery, which is why reverse pipetting is recommended for viscous or foaming liquids such as glycerol or detergent solutions.

commonMistakes: Making up to the final volume with water before dissolving, so the concentration is lower than calculated; or adding the full volume of water and then adjusting the pH with large volumes of acid.
Adjusting the pH at room temperature of a Tris buffer that will be used on ice, so the working pH is off by half a unit or more.
Using a P1000 for 50 microlitres or a P20 for 18 microlitres at the extreme end of its range, where accuracy is poor.
Dipping the pH meter electrode into a stock bottle and contaminating it, or storing the electrode dry.

units.title: Spectrophotometry and the Beer-Lambert Law
units.hook: Light passing through a coloured solution is a quiet ruler: the less comes out, the more is inside. Almost every number you will report in this course, from protein concentration to enzyme activity to DNA yield, comes from asking how much light a solution swallowed.
learningObjectives: Define transmittance and absorbance and convert between them.
Apply the Beer-Lambert law (A = epsilon x c x l) to find a concentration from an absorbance.
Operate a spectrophotometer: choose wavelength and cuvette, blank, and measure samples.
Record an absorption spectrum and choose lambda-max for an assay.
Recognise when absorbance data fall outside the reliable linear range and how to correct for it.

keyConcepts.definition: The fraction of incident light that passes through the sample, I divided by I0.
A = -log10(T). It is dimensionless and additive for independent absorbers; an absorbance of 1 means 10% of the light gets through.
A = epsilon x c x l: absorbance is proportional to the molar absorption coefficient, the concentration and the path length.
A property of a compound at a given wavelength and conditions, in L per mol per cm. NADH at 340 nm has epsilon of about 6220 L/mol/cm.
A sample containing everything except the absorbing species, used to set zero absorbance and subtract the contribution of buffer, reagents and cuvette.
A plot of absorbance against wavelength; the peak (lambda-max) is usually the most sensitive wavelength to measure.
The concentration range where A is truly proportional to c; in practice measurements between roughly 0.1 and 1.0 absorbance units are the most reliable.
Light of the wrong wavelength reaching the detector, which makes high absorbance readings plateau below their true values.

deeper.beginner: A spectrophotometer shines light of one chosen wavelength through your sample in a cuvette and measures how much comes out the other side. First put in a blank (the buffer and reagents without your compound) and press zero so the instrument ignores everything that is not your compound. Then read your samples. Use plastic or glass cuvettes for visible light and quartz for ultraviolet below about 340 nm, hold them by the frosted sides and wipe the clear faces. If the reading is above about 1.5, dilute the sample and read again.
deeper.intermediate: If you know epsilon you can calculate concentration directly from a single reading, but in practice a calibration (standard) curve of A against known concentrations is more robust because it accounts for the instrument and conditions. Deviations from Beer's law arise from high concentrations (molecular interactions and refractive-index effects), chemical equilibria such as association or dissociation that change with concentration, and light scattering by turbid samples, which looks like absorbance. Choose lambda-max for the best sensitivity, but if a peak is very sharp choose a wavelength on a flatter region to reduce errors due to small wavelength calibration offsets. Always check that the reference and sample cuvettes are matched and that the sample is free of bubbles and fingerprints.
deeper.advanced: Absorbance measurements have their best signal-to-noise ratio at moderate values: at low A the relative error from small intensity noise is large, and at high A too little light reaches the detector, so the relative concentration error is smallest around A of 0.4 to 0.5 for typical instruments. Scattering from cells or precipitates (optical density at 600 nm) is empirical and instrument dependent rather than Beer-Lambert absorbance, so calibration against cell counts or dry mass is needed for each instrument. Multicomponent mixtures can be resolved by measuring at several wavelengths and solving simultaneous equations if the epsilons are known, as is done for nucleic acid and protein mixtures with A260 and A280, and derivative or diode-array techniques can resolve overlapping bands. Microvolume instruments use very short path lengths (about 1 mm or less) so that concentrated samples can be measured without dilution, but their reproducibility is limited by pipetting of the 1 to 2 microlitre sample.

commonMistakes: Blanking with water when the sample is in a coloured buffer or contains reagent that itself absorbs.
Reading very concentrated samples above an absorbance of about 2 and still using Beer's law without dilution.
Using a plastic or glass cuvette for ultraviolet measurements, where the cuvette itself absorbs light.
Handling the clear sides of a cuvette or leaving fingerprints and air bubbles in the light path.

units.title: Protein Quantification and Standard Curves
units.hook: You cannot compare two preparations, load an equal amount on a gel or report enzyme activity per milligram if you do not know how much protein you have. A clear, honest protein assay is the unglamorous number that every other result in the lab leans on.
learningObjectives: Compare the principles, ranges and interferences of the Bradford, BCA, Lowry and direct A280 methods.
Prepare a dilution series of a standard protein and construct a standard curve.
Calculate the concentration of an unknown from a standard curve, accounting for dilution.
Choose an assay compatible with the buffer components in your sample.
Explain why different proteins give different responses and what this means for accuracy.

keyConcepts.definition: Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 binds mainly to basic and aromatic residues, shifting its absorbance maximum from about 465 to 595 nm. Fast and cheap, but sensitive to detergents.

Protein reduces Cu(2+) to Cu(+) in alkaline solution (the biuret reaction), and bicinchoninic acid chelates Cu(+) to give a purple product read near 562 nm. Tolerates most detergents but not reducing agents.
A biuret step followed by reduction of the Folin-Ciocalteu reagent by copper-treated protein and tyrosine and tryptophan residues; read near 750 nm. Sensitive but with many interferences.
Aromatic residues (mainly tryptophan and tyrosine) absorb at 280 nm, so a pure protein can be quantified directly if its extinction coefficient is known.
Absorbance of known concentrations of a reference protein, usually bovine serum albumin (BSA), fitted by a line or curve and used to read unknowns.
Assays respond differently to different proteins because they depend on amino acid composition, so a BSA-based value is an estimate for other proteins.
Components of the sample buffer (detergents, reducing agents, chelators, sugars) that change the colour development and bias the result.

deeper.beginner: Make a set of tubes with BSA at known concentrations, add the assay reagent to them and to your unknown samples, wait the stated time and read absorbance. Plot absorbance (y) against concentration (x), draw the best-fit line and read the concentration of your sample from the line. If the unknown reads above your top standard, dilute the sample and repeat, then multiply the answer by the dilution factor.
deeper.intermediate: Make the standards in the same buffer as the samples so that background and interfering substances are matched, include a blank, and run everything in duplicate or triplicate. Bradford typically gives a slightly curved response, so fit a quadratic or use only the linear segment; BCA and Lowry are closer to linear but are time and temperature dependent, so incubate standards and unknowns together. Choose the assay by the sample: SDS in a lysis buffer interferes with Bradford but not BCA, while DTT or beta-mercaptoethanol interferes with BCA and Lowry. Reporting that protein concentration was measured against a BSA standard, and not that it is the true protein concentration, is more honest.
deeper.advanced: Extinction-coefficient-based methods (A280 using a value calculated from the amino acid sequence) are accurate for pure proteins but not for mixtures, nucleic acid contamination biases A280 upward (a correction using A260/A280 is only approximate), and fluorescence-based or amino-acid-analysis methods approach absolute accuracy. Bradford response depends strongly on arginine content and on sample pH, and detergents change the dye aggregation state; BCA response includes contributions from cysteine, tyrosine and tryptophan side chains and the peptide backbone. Because neither assay is truly absolute, comparisons across samples are meaningful only if the same assay, standard and conditions are used, and orthogonal confirmation (for example staining of a gel loaded with equal measured amounts) is good practice before quantitative claims are made.

commonMistakes: Preparing standards in water but measuring samples in a detergent-containing buffer, so the standard curve does not apply.
Extrapolating beyond the highest standard instead of diluting the sample.
Forcing a straight line through a visibly curved standard curve, giving large errors at the ends.
Forgetting to multiply by the dilution factor, or reading samples at different times after reagent addition.

units.title: Centrifugation and Cell Fractionation
units.hook: Spin a homogenised liver and, with nothing more than gravity multiplied a few thousand times, the cell sorts itself: nuclei first, then mitochondria, then membrane vesicles, then the soluble cytosol. The same simple physics underpins everything from clinical blood tubes to purifying viruses.
learningObjectives: Explain how sedimentation depends on particle size, density, solvent density and viscosity, and the applied force.
Convert between rpm and relative centrifugal force (xg) for a given rotor radius.
Plan a differential centrifugation scheme to prepare nuclear, mitochondrial, microsomal and cytosolic fractions.
Distinguish rate-zonal from isopycnic density gradient centrifugation and give uses of each.
Use marker enzymes to judge the purity of a subcellular fraction.

keyConcepts.definition: The acceleration expressed in multiples of g. RCF depends on rotor radius and the square of rotational speed, so rpm alone is not transferable between rotors.
Disrupting tissue or cells in a cold, buffered, isotonic medium (often sucrose) so that organelles stay intact.
Sequential spins at increasing force; each pellet is enriched for the next smaller class of particles and the supernatant is respun.
Layering a sample on a gradient of sucrose, Percoll or caesium chloride to separate particles by size (rate-zonal) or by buoyant density (isopycnic).
An enzyme or protein specific to one organelle, for example succinate dehydrogenase in mitochondria, used to follow the organelle through a fractionation.
Fixed-angle rotors pellet quickly; swing-bucket rotors keep tubes horizontal during the run, which suits gradients.
After a spin, the material that sediments is the pellet and the liquid left behind is the supernatant.

deeper.beginner: Cut the tissue into small pieces on ice, add cold isotonic buffer, and homogenise gently. Spin at low speed to pellet nuclei and unbroken cells, transfer the supernatant to a fresh tube and spin faster to pellet mitochondria, then faster again for microsomes. What is left is mostly cytosol. Always balance tubes opposite one another in the rotor and keep everything cold to slow protein degradation.
deeper.intermediate: Use the conversion RCF = 1.118 x 10^-5 x r (cm) x rpm^2 to translate protocols between centrifuges, using the radius of the sample. A typical scheme uses roughly 600 to 1000 xg for nuclei and debris, about 10,000 xg for mitochondria and lysosomes, and about 100,000 xg (ultracentrifuge) for microsomes, which are the vesicles formed from fragmented endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane; exact values depend on tissue and protocol. Fractions are contaminated by their neighbours, so purity is checked by enzyme assays (succinate dehydrogenase, catalase, acid phosphatase, glucose-6-phosphatase, lactate dehydrogenase) or antibody markers and expressed as recovery and enrichment. Use protease inhibitors and keep the medium isotonic to avoid organelle swelling and lysis.
deeper.advanced: Sedimentation follows Svedberg's analysis: the sedimentation coefficient s is proportional to particle mass times the factor (1 minus the partial specific volume times the solvent density), divided by the frictional coefficient. Particles whose density equals the medium do not sediment, which is the basis of isopycnic banding in gradients such as caesium chloride, famously used by Meselson and Stahl to separate DNA of different nitrogen isotope composition. Rate-zonal separations must be stopped before the fastest species reaches the bottom, whereas isopycnic separations are run to equilibrium. Modern workflows often supplement or replace differential centrifugation with density gradients, affinity capture of organelles or proximity labelling, because differential spins yield enriched rather than pure fractions.

commonMistakes: Quoting rpm without the rotor type or radius, so the protocol cannot be reproduced on another centrifuge.
Running an unbalanced rotor or filling tubes beyond the maximum volume.
Assuming a pellet is a single pure organelle; fractions are enriched, not pure.
Letting homogenate warm up or using a hypotonic buffer that bursts organelles.

units.title: Chromatography: TLC, Column and Protein Purification
units.hook: A chromatography column is a very long, very patient race in which molecules differ in how much they like the track and how much they like the solvent. That small difference in preference, repeated thousands of times, is how a single protein is pulled out of a cell's worth of thousands.
learningObjectives: Explain the principle of partitioning between a stationary and a mobile phase.
Run and interpret a thin-layer chromatogram and calculate Rf values.
Describe how ion exchange, size exclusion (gel filtration), affinity and hydrophobic interaction chromatography each separate proteins.
Design a simple multi-step purification and track it in a purification table.
Choose an appropriate buffer pH and salt for ion exchange given the protein's pI.

keyConcepts.definition: The fixed material (silica, resin) and the moving solvent. Separation arises because compounds spend different fractions of time in each phase.
In TLC, the distance moved by a spot divided by the distance moved by the solvent front. It is characteristic of a compound under fixed conditions.

Proteins bind to charged resin through their net charge. Above its pI a protein is negatively charged and binds an anion exchanger (for example Q or DEAE); below its pI it binds a cation exchanger (for example S or CM). Elution is by increasing salt or changing pH.
Porous beads let small molecules enter and so travel a longer path; large molecules are excluded and elute first, in order of decreasing size.

A ligand with specific binding to the target is coupled to the resin, for example nickel-NTA for His-tagged proteins, glutathione for GST fusions or an antibody for an antigen. Elution is by competing ligand (such as imidazole) or a change of conditions.
Separation based on hydrophobicity, with HIC binding at high salt and reversed-phase HPLC using organic solvents; the latter is widely used for peptides.
A record of total protein, total activity, specific activity, yield and fold-purification at each step, used to judge how well a scheme works.
High-performance liquid chromatography uses small particles and high pressure for faster, higher-resolution separations coupled to detectors such as UV absorbance.

deeper.beginner: In TLC, draw a pencil line near the bottom of a silica plate, spot your samples, and stand the plate in a shallow pool of solvent. As the solvent rises it carries compounds with it; polar compounds stick more to polar silica and move less. Mark the solvent front, develop the spots (UV, iodine, or ninhydrin for amino acids), and calculate Rf. For proteins in a column, the sample is loaded onto the top, buffer is passed through, and fractions are collected and tested for the protein of interest.
deeper.intermediate: A typical protein purification begins with clarification (centrifugation), a capture step (affinity or ion exchange, to concentrate and remove most contaminants), an intermediate step (often ion exchange), and a polishing step (gel filtration, which also tells you the oligomeric state and exchanges the buffer). Choose pH about one unit away from the pI so the protein carries a clear charge, start with low salt for binding, and elute with a salt gradient so peaks come off in order of binding strength. Gel filtration resolves by hydrodynamic size rather than strict molecular weight, and must be calibrated with standards of known size, so it is run last and loaded in a small volume (typically a few percent of the column volume) to preserve resolution. Throughout, assay activity and protein at each step to build the purification table.
deeper.advanced: Resolution depends on selectivity, efficiency (plate number) and retention; narrow peaks need small particles, even packing, low flow rates and minimal extra-column volume. For gel filtration the partition coefficient Kav = (Ve - V0)/(Vt - V0) is approximately linear in the logarithm of molecular weight for globular proteins, so elution volumes of standards give a calibration curve, although non-globular or interacting proteins deviate. Affinity tags simplify purification but can alter folding, activity or oligomerisation, so tags are often removed by a specific protease. Purification of membrane proteins requires detergents that replace lipids and must be kept above the critical micelle concentration throughout. Strategy is increasingly driven by automated FPLC systems and analytical methods such as dynamic light scattering and mass spectrometry to verify purity and identity.

commonMistakes: Marking the TLC baseline with a pen whose ink runs, or immersing the baseline in solvent so the spots dissolve.
Loading too large a volume or too concentrated a sample onto a gel filtration column, ruining resolution.
Choosing an ion exchange resin of the wrong charge for the buffer pH relative to the protein's pI.
Allowing a column to run dry or introducing air bubbles, which cause channelling and poor separation.

units.title: Protein Electrophoresis: SDS-PAGE and Western Blotting
units.hook: A single stained gel can show you whether a purification worked, whether a protein is the size it should be, and whether an antibody is telling the truth. Learning to run and read one is a rite of passage in every protein lab.
learningObjectives: Explain how SDS and a reducing agent let proteins be separated by size alone.
Describe the roles of the stacking and resolving gels in the Laemmli system.
Prepare, load and run an SDS-polyacrylamide gel and choose a suitable acrylamide percentage.
Estimate molecular weight from a standard curve of log(MW) against migration distance.
Describe the steps of a western blot and the controls needed to interpret one.

keyConcepts.definition: Sodium dodecyl sulfate is an anionic detergent that denatures proteins and coats them with negative charge roughly in proportion to their length, so they separate by size.
Dithiothreitol or 2-mercaptoethanol breaks disulfide bonds so that subunits and chains run separately.
A cross-linked mesh formed by acrylamide and bis-acrylamide with APS and TEMED as initiators. Higher percentage means smaller pores, resolving smaller proteins.
A large-pore stacking gel at about pH 6.8 concentrates proteins into a sharp band before they enter the resolving gel at about pH 8.8.
A mixture of proteins of known size (a ladder) run alongside samples for calibration.
Proteins separated by gel are transferred to a nitrocellulose or PVDF membrane and detected with a specific primary antibody and an enzyme- or fluorophore-labelled secondary antibody.
Saturating unoccupied binding sites on the membrane with milk protein or BSA to reduce nonspecific antibody binding.
A housekeeping protein or total-protein stain used to confirm that equal amounts of sample were loaded and transferred.

deeper.beginner: Mix your protein with sample buffer containing SDS, a reducing agent, glycerol and tracking dye, heat it to unfold the protein, and load it into wells in the gel. Apply voltage: negatively charged proteins move toward the positive electrode, smaller ones faster. Stop before the dye front runs off, then stain with Coomassie to see bands. For a western blot, move the proteins onto a membrane, block, incubate with antibodies and add substrate to make the band light up.
deeper.intermediate: Choose 12 to 15 percent gels for small proteins (under about 30 kDa), 8 to 10 percent for mid-sized proteins and gradient gels for a wide range; load equal protein, not equal volume, based on your assay. In the Laemmli discontinuous system, chloride (leading) and glycine (trailing) ions set up a moving boundary that stacks proteins into a narrow zone, and at the higher pH of the resolving gel glycine becomes more negatively charged and overtakes the proteins, which then separate by size. Plot log molecular weight against relative mobility (Rf) of the marker bands to estimate sizes of unknowns, and be aware that glycoproteins and membrane proteins can run anomalously. In the blot, transfer efficiency depends on size and time, PVDF requires wetting with methanol, antibody dilutions and washes control background, and a loading control or total-protein stain is necessary before comparing signal intensities.
deeper.advanced: SDS binds at roughly 1.4 g per gram of protein, giving a nearly constant charge-to-mass ratio, but highly acidic, basic or heavily modified proteins deviate, and membrane proteins can aggregate if heated. Western blots are semi-quantitative unless the signal is shown to be within the linear dynamic range of detection; enhanced chemiluminescence saturates and film is non-linear, so fluorescent secondaries and total-protein normalisation are increasingly preferred. Antibody validation is a major source of irreproducibility: the band at the expected size is not proof of specificity, and knockout or knockdown controls, peptide competition and orthogonal methods are used to establish it. Alternatives or complements include native PAGE, two-dimensional gels (isoelectric focusing followed by SDS-PAGE), capillary western systems and mass spectrometry for identification.

commonMistakes: Unpolymerised acrylamide is a neurotoxin; weighing powder in the open or touching wet gel without gloves is a safety error.
Loading equal volumes of samples that differ in concentration and then interpreting band intensity as expression difference.
Running the gel too long so that small proteins run off, or too hot so that bands smile and distort.
Using a loading control that itself changes under the experimental condition, or one that is saturated.

units.title: Enzyme Assays and Kinetics
units.hook: An enzyme is invisible, but it announces itself by what it changes. Learning to follow a reaction as colour or light appearing in a cuvette lets you measure how fast a catalyst works, how it responds to substrate, and what a drug does to it.
learningObjectives: Design a continuous spectrophotometric assay and choose suitable blanks and controls.
Measure initial velocities and convert absorbance change to rate using the Beer-Lambert law.
Define units of activity and specific activity and calculate them.
Determine Km and Vmax from a substrate series by non-linear regression and by linearised plots, and explain the limitations of the latter.
Interpret inhibition patterns and the effect of pH and temperature.

keyConcepts.definition: The rate measured early in the reaction, in the linear phase, when substrate is barely depleted and product has not yet accumulated or inhibited the enzyme.
One unit (U) is the amount of enzyme that converts 1 micromole of substrate per minute under stated conditions; the SI unit is the katal (mol per second).
Units of activity per milligram of protein, a measure of purity that rises as contaminants are removed.
Vmax is the maximal rate at saturating substrate; Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax; kcat = Vmax divided by enzyme concentration.
Continuous assays read signal in real time (for example NADH at 340 nm); discontinuous assays stop the reaction at set times and measure product afterwards.
No-enzyme and no-substrate tubes reveal spontaneous reaction and background signal that must be subtracted.
Competitive inhibitors raise apparent Km without changing Vmax; uncompetitive lower both; non-competitive (pure) lower Vmax with unchanged Km.
Activity depends on pH, temperature, ionic strength and cofactors; the optimum is where the enzyme is both active and stable.

deeper.beginner: Mix buffer, substrate and enzyme in a cuvette, start the clock when the last component goes in, and read absorbance every few seconds. Plot absorbance against time; the straight, early part gives the rate. Convert the slope to micromoles per minute using epsilon and path length, then divide by the amount of protein for specific activity. Repeat at several substrate concentrations to see the rate level off.
deeper.intermediate: For valid Michaelis-Menten kinetics the enzyme concentration must be much lower than substrate, and less than about 10 percent of substrate should be consumed during the measurement. Common reporter systems are NAD(P)H at 340 nm (epsilon 6220 per M per cm), p-nitrophenol released from p-nitrophenyl phosphate at 405 nm (epsilon depends on pH, so alkaline stop solution is used for fixed-time assays), and o-nitrophenol from ONPG for beta-galactosidase at 420 nm. Fit v against [S] by non-linear regression to get Km and Vmax with confidence intervals; the Lineweaver-Burk plot is useful for visualising inhibition type, but it distorts errors by weighting low-substrate points heavily and should not be used for fitting. Include temperature control and pre-incubation, and report assay conditions fully because parameters are only meaningful with them.
deeper.advanced: The Michaelis-Menten equation is derived under steady-state or rapid-equilibrium assumptions that fail at high enzyme concentration, for tight-binding inhibitors (where Morrison analysis is used) and for multi-substrate or allosteric enzymes, which need more general rate laws. Fitting progress curves to the integrated rate equation can extract parameters from a single time course but requires that product inhibition and enzyme instability are absent. Km values are condition-dependent and not a pure measure of affinity, since Km equals the dissociation constant only when catalysis is slow relative to dissociation. For inhibitor studies, IC50 depends on substrate concentration and is related to Ki by the Cheng-Prusoff equation. Reporting standards such as STRENDA exist so that kinetic data can be reproduced and reused.

commonMistakes: Measuring a rate over a time window where the progress curve has already bent, so the rate is underestimated.
Starting the reaction with the wrong component (for example enzyme added last in one tube and substrate last in another) so pre-incubation differs.
Using Lineweaver-Burk regression to estimate Km and Vmax from noisy data.
Forgetting to correct for a non-enzymatic background rate seen in the no-enzyme control.

units.title: DNA and RNA Extraction and Quantification
units.hook: DNA is chemically hardy but RNA is fragile, and the room is full of enzymes that destroy it. Getting clean, intact nucleic acids out of cells is partly chemistry and partly discipline, and every downstream experiment, from PCR to sequencing, depends on how well you do it.
learningObjectives: Describe the steps of a nucleic acid extraction: lysis, deproteinisation, precipitation or binding, washing and elution.
Explain the role of detergent, proteinase K, EDTA, phenol-chloroform, salt and alcohol.
Compare organic extraction, silica spin-column and magnetic bead methods.
Apply RNase-free technique and extract RNA with a guanidinium-phenol reagent.
Quantify nucleic acids by A260 and assess purity from A260/A280 and A260/A230.

keyConcepts.definition: Breaking cells open with detergent, enzymes (lysozyme, proteinase K) or mechanical force to release nucleic acids.
A chelator that removes Mg2+, which DNases require for activity, protecting DNA during extraction.
Denatured proteins collect at the interphase and organic phase while nucleic acids stay in the aqueous phase. At acidic pH, DNA moves into the organic phase and RNA stays in water.
In the presence of monovalent cations (for example sodium acetate), ethanol or isopropanol makes nucleic acids insoluble so they can be pelleted and washed in 70% ethanol.
In high concentrations of chaotropic salts, nucleic acids bind silica; after washing with ethanol buffer, they are eluted in low-salt buffer or water.
Heat-stable, cofactor-free enzymes found on skin and surfaces; RNA work needs gloves, RNase-free tips and reagents and dedicated space.
A rough purity check: around 1.8 is typical of pure DNA and about 2.0 of pure RNA; lower values suggest protein or phenol contamination.
Expected to be about 2.0 to 2.2 for clean nucleic acid; low values point to carryover of salts, phenol, guanidine or carbohydrates.

deeper.beginner: Break the cells open in a buffer containing detergent, which dissolves membranes, and protect the DNA from enzymes that would cut it. Separate DNA from protein, add salt and cold ethanol and DNA appears as pale threads that can be spun into a pellet. Wash the pellet in 70 percent ethanol and dissolve it in buffer. For RNA, wear gloves, use RNase-free tubes and water, and keep samples cold or frozen.
deeper.intermediate: Organic extraction with phenol:chloroform:isoamyl alcohol (25:24:1) gives high yields but uses hazardous solvents; silica columns are fast and give clean preparations with lower yield; magnetic beads suit automation. Proteinase K digests nucleases and proteins in the presence of SDS and EDTA. For RNA, acid guanidinium thiocyanate-phenol-chloroform (TRIzol-type reagents) denatures RNases immediately and separates RNA into the aqueous phase, DNA to the interphase, and protein to the organic phase; RNA is precipitated with isopropanol and washed with 75 percent ethanol. Plasmid minipreps rely on alkaline lysis: NaOH with SDS lyses cells and denatures DNA, then potassium acetate neutralises, so chromosomal DNA and protein-SDS complexes precipitate while the small plasmid renatures and stays in solution. Measure concentration by A260 (about 50 micrograms per mL of double-stranded DNA and 40 per mL of RNA per absorbance unit) and check integrity on a gel; for RNA the 28S and 18S ribosomal bands should be sharp with the larger roughly twice the intensity of the smaller for mammalian samples.
deeper.advanced: A260 reports all nucleic acids and free nucleotides, so RNA contaminates DNA estimates and vice versa, and ratios are influenced by pH and instrument; fluorescent dyes (PicoGreen, Qubit assays) are selective for double-stranded DNA or RNA and more sensitive. Integrity is quantified by capillary electrophoresis, giving RNA integrity numbers, which predict suitability for RNA-seq and RT-qPCR. Silica binding works by chaotropic disruption of water structure and dehydration of the nucleic acid, allowing adsorption to silica; this is the Boom method that underlies most commercial kits. Extraction bias is real: methods differ in recovery of small RNAs, high-molecular-weight DNA and DNA from Gram-positive bacteria or plants rich in polysaccharides and polyphenols, requiring tailored lysis (for example CTAB). For long-read sequencing, gentle handling to avoid shearing is critical.

commonMistakes: Touching RNase-sensitive reagents with bare hands or non-certified tips and then wondering why the RNA smears.
Pipetting from the interphase along with the aqueous layer, carrying protein and phenol into the sample.
Over-drying the pellet so that it will not redissolve, or failing to remove ethanol before eluting.
Trusting A260/A280 as proof of purity when A260/A230 is low or RNA contamination is present.

units.title: Agarose Gel Electrophoresis of DNA
units.hook: A band of glowing DNA on a gel is the quickest honest answer to the question: did it work? Learn to read a gel and you can check an extraction, a PCR, a digest and a ligation in under an hour.
learningObjectives: Explain why DNA migrates through agarose and how fragment size affects its mobility.
Prepare an agarose gel of appropriate percentage and choose TAE or TBE running buffer.
Load, run and visualise a gel safely with a DNA ladder and loading dye.
Estimate fragment sizes from a semi-logarithmic plot of size against distance.
Recognise supercoiled, linear and nicked plasmid forms and common artefacts.

keyConcepts.definition: The phosphate backbone gives DNA a uniform negative charge per unit length, so in an electric field it moves toward the anode and the gel matrix sorts it by size.
Lower percentages (0.7 to 1%) resolve large fragments; higher (2 to 3%) resolve small fragments.
Within a gel's working range, migration distance is approximately linear in the logarithm of fragment length.
A mixture of fragments of known sizes run in a lane to calibrate unknown bands.
Ethidium bromide and safer alternatives such as SYBR Safe bind DNA and fluoresce under UV or blue light; ethidium is a mutagen and requires careful handling.
Contains glycerol or sucrose to weigh the sample down and tracking dyes (bromophenol blue, xylene cyanol) to monitor migration.
Supercoiled plasmids usually run fastest, linear next, and nicked (open circular) slowest, although exact order depends on gel conditions.
TAE (Tris-acetate-EDTA) suits large fragments and DNA recovery; TBE (Tris-borate-EDTA) buffers better and sharpens small fragments, but borate can inhibit some enzymes.

deeper.beginner: Melt agarose in running buffer, let it cool a little, add a DNA stain, pour it into a tray with a comb and let it set. Put the gel in the tank covered by buffer, load samples mixed with loading dye alongside a ladder, and run at a moderate voltage until the dye has moved most of the way. DNA moves from black (negative) to red (positive). Image the gel and compare your bands with the ladder.
deeper.intermediate: Choose agarose concentration for the size range you need and run at about 5 to 8 volts per centimetre between electrodes; higher voltage heats the gel and smears bands. Do not overload: more than a few hundred nanograms in a band makes it broad and may hide minor products. Compare expected and observed sizes by plotting log size against distance for the ladder; sizes of unknown fragments are read from the line. Interpret smears (degraded DNA or too much sample), primer-dimers (very small, fast bands in PCR), and extra bands in plasmid preps as different topologies. Always include a negative control lane when interpreting PCR products and photograph the gel with a scale or ladder visible for the record.
deeper.advanced: Mobility depends on the ratio of charge to frictional drag and on the reptation of DNA through pores, which for long fragments under constant field becomes size-independent (above about 20 to 50 kilobases), so pulsed-field electrophoresis, which periodically changes field direction, is used for very large DNA. Intercalating dyes alter mobility and can change the apparent order of topological forms; running a gel with and without dye distinguishes them. The buffers differ in ionic strength and conductivity, so run time and heat generation vary; recirculation helps for long runs. Gel images are quantifiable only within the linear response range of the camera, so reporting relative band intensity from saturated images is invalid, while fluorometric methods and capillary electrophoresis (bioanalysers) provide more precise sizing and quantification.

commonMistakes: Running the gel with the wells at the positive end, so the DNA runs backward off the gel.
Overloading lanes or loading too little, giving smeared or invisible bands.
Using old running buffer that has become depleted of ions and pH, causing poor resolution and heating.
Exposing yourself to UV light without a face shield or glass cover, or disposing of ethidium-containing gels in ordinary waste.

units.title: PCR and Quantitative PCR
units.hook: Heat, cool, copy: repeat thirty times and a single molecule becomes a billion. PCR turned DNA from something studied in bulk into something that can be searched for, cut out, sequenced or counted in a drop of sample.
learningObjectives: Explain the three steps of a PCR cycle and the exponential nature of amplification.
Design primers and choose annealing temperature and extension time.
Set up a PCR with appropriate positive, negative and no-template controls.
Distinguish end-point PCR, RT-PCR and quantitative real-time PCR.
Interpret qPCR amplification curves, Ct values, melt curves and relative expression by the delta-delta Ct method.

keyConcepts.definition: Denaturation (about 95 degrees Celsius) separates strands, annealing (about 50 to 65 degrees) lets primers bind, and extension (72 degrees for Taq) lets the polymerase copy the template.
Short synthetic oligonucleotides, typically 18 to 25 bases, flanking the target region; they should have similar melting temperatures, avoid self-complementarity and end in G or C.
Taq polymerase survives denaturation but lacks proofreading; high-fidelity enzymes (Pfu, Q5) have 3' to 5' exonuclease activity and make fewer errors.
Mg2+ is a polymerase cofactor and affects specificity; dNTPs are the building blocks, typically about 200 micromolar each.
A no-template control reveals contamination; a positive control shows the reaction can work; a no-RT control checks genomic DNA contamination in RT-PCR.
RNA is first copied into cDNA by reverse transcriptase, then amplified, allowing gene expression to be measured.
A fluorescent signal (intercalating dye such as SYBR Green or a sequence-specific probe) is measured each cycle; the cycle at which it crosses a threshold (Ct) relates to starting amount.
The fraction by which template increases per cycle; a perfect reaction doubles each cycle (100%), corresponding to a standard-curve slope of about -3.32.

deeper.beginner: In a PCR tube you mix the template DNA, two primers, nucleotides, polymerase and buffer. A thermal cycler repeats a three-temperature cycle: first heat splits the DNA strands, then cooling lets primers stick to their matching places, then warming allows the polymerase to build new strands. After n cycles, the target is amplified roughly 2 to the power n times, so 30 cycles gives about a billion-fold increase. Run a sample on a gel to see a band of the expected size, and always include a tube with no template as a contamination check.
deeper.intermediate: Set annealing temperature a few degrees below the lower primer Tm, extension time about one minute per kilobase for Taq, and 25 to 35 cycles; too many cycles lead to non-specific products and plateau as reagents deplete. Optimise by gradient PCR, adjusting Mg2+, or using hot-start enzymes to prevent primer-dimers. In qPCR, lower Ct means more starting template; with 100 percent efficiency, a difference of about 3.3 cycles equals a tenfold difference. Check specificity by melt curve (a single sharp peak) and measure efficiency from a serial dilution. In relative quantification by the delta-delta Ct method, normalise the target Ct to a validated reference gene in each sample, then compare treated and control; it assumes similar, near-100 percent efficiencies for target and reference.
deeper.advanced: Amplification is exponential only in the early cycles; later, enzyme and primer limitation and product re-annealing cause a plateau, so end-point band intensity is not quantitative. Reference-gene stability must be validated under your conditions, since commonly used housekeeping genes can change with treatment, and multiple references are recommended. Rigorous qPCR follows the MIQE guidelines, which require reporting of sample handling, RNA quality, primer sequences, efficiency, and replicate structure, because many published qPCR results are not reproducible when this is omitted. Digital PCR partitions the reaction into thousands of droplets or wells and counts positives, giving absolute quantification without a standard curve. Contamination by amplicons is a constant risk and is controlled by physical separation of pre- and post-PCR areas, filter tips, and sometimes uracil-DNA glycosylase carry-over prevention.

commonMistakes: Setting up PCR in the same area and with the same pipettes used to handle amplified products, leading to contamination.
Using an annealing temperature that is too low, giving multiple bands, or too high, giving no product.
Interpreting band brightness from a 35-cycle PCR as a quantitative measure of starting amount.
Using a single unvalidated reference gene for delta-delta Ct and assuming no efficiency differences.

selfCheck.question: If a PCR doubles the amount of target every cycle, roughly what fold-increase does 10 cycles give?

selfCheck.question: In qPCR, sample A has a Ct of 22 and sample B a Ct of 25 for the same gene, with 100% efficiency. Sample A contains approximately:

units.title: Cloning: Restriction Digestion, Ligation and Transformation
units.hook: Cut a plasmid, paste in a gene, put it into bacteria and let a billion cells copy it. Recombinant DNA technology looks like molecular scissors and glue, but its real power is the screening step that tells you which colony contains the construct you actually wanted.
learningObjectives: Plan a cloning strategy with compatible restriction sites and a suitable vector.
Set up and analyse restriction digests, including diagnostic digests of plasmid preps.
Perform a ligation with an appropriate vector to insert ratio and suitable controls.
Transform competent E. coli and select recombinants using antibiotics and blue-white screening.
Verify clones by colony PCR, restriction analysis and sequencing.

keyConcepts.definition: A bacterial endonuclease that cuts DNA at a specific palindromic sequence, such as EcoRI at G^AATTC, leaving sticky (cohesive) or blunt ends.
A plasmid carrying an origin of replication, a selectable marker such as ampicillin resistance, and a multiple cloning site.
T4 DNA ligase uses ATP to form phosphodiester bonds between compatible ends, joining insert to vector.
Using two different restriction enzymes so that the insert can only enter the vector in one orientation and the vector cannot easily self-ligate.
Removing 5' phosphates from a singly cut vector prevents it re-closing on itself, reducing background colonies.
Bacteria treated (for example with calcium chloride) or prepared (electrocompetent) so that they take up DNA; heat shock at about 42 degrees Celsius for under a minute aids uptake.

Insertion of DNA into the lacZ-alpha fragment of the vector disrupts beta-galactosidase alpha-complementation, so recombinant colonies stay white on X-gal and IPTG plates while non-recombinants turn blue.
Colonies obtained per microgram of control plasmid DNA, a measure of how good your competent cells and technique are.

deeper.beginner: Choose a vector and cut both vector and insert DNA with the same restriction enzyme or enzymes, so their ends fit. Mix them with ligase, which joins them into a single circular molecule. Put the mixture into competent bacteria, let them recover in rich broth and plate them on agar containing an antibiotic. Only cells that took up a plasmid with the resistance gene grow into colonies. Pick several colonies and check which ones really carry your insert.
deeper.intermediate: Cut vector and insert to completion, purify them from the digest (gel extraction or column), and ligate at a vector-to-insert molar ratio from about 1:3 to 1:5, calculated from the sizes of each piece. Run control ligations: vector alone without ligase shows undigested background, vector with ligase but no insert shows self-ligation, and a transformation with an intact plasmid reports efficiency. Heat shock at 42 degrees Celsius for 30 to 60 seconds, return to ice, recover in antibiotic-free medium for about an hour, then plate. Pick white colonies, grow minipreps, and verify by diagnostic digest with an enzyme that gives a different pattern with and without insert; confirm the sequence of the insert and junctions by Sanger sequencing.
deeper.advanced: Classical restriction-ligation is increasingly supplemented by seamless methods: Gibson assembly uses an exonuclease, polymerase and ligase to join overlapping fragments; Golden Gate uses type IIS enzymes that cut outside their recognition site to enable scarless multi-fragment assembly; recombination-based systems (Gateway) and ligation-independent cloning reduce reliance on available restriction sites. Transformation efficiency of chemically competent cells is typically 10^6 to 10^8 colonies per microgram, and of electrocompetent cells 10^9 or higher; large plasmids and ligation products transform less efficiently than supercoiled controls. Choice of E. coli strain matters: recA-negative strains reduce recombination, endA-negative strains improve plasmid quality, and some constructs (repeats, toxic genes) need low-copy vectors or special strains. Verification by sequencing is non-negotiable, as PCR-derived inserts and passaged clones can acquire mutations.

commonMistakes: Digesting with enzymes that are not active in the same buffer, or heat-inactivating when the enzyme is not heat labile.
Not purifying the digested vector, so small removed fragments or uncut plasmid inflate background colonies.
Plating the whole transformation without checking the antibiotic, its concentration or whether it was added to molten agar that was too hot.
Assuming that every white colony contains the right insert and skipping verification.

units.title: Data Analysis, Uncertainty and Scientific Reporting
units.hook: A measurement without an error estimate is an opinion. The last step of every experiment is deciding what your numbers can honestly claim, and then writing it so a reader can judge the evidence for themselves.
learningObjectives: Distinguish accuracy from precision and systematic from random error.
Calculate mean, standard deviation and standard error and choose which to plot.
Distinguish technical from biological replicates and explain why pseudoreplication is a problem.
Fit and interpret a calibration curve or non-linear model, and report parameters with uncertainty.
Perform and interpret a t-test and avoid common errors with p-values.
Structure a laboratory report (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion) with clear figures and tables.

keyConcepts.definition: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is repeatability. A well-calibrated instrument can be precise but wrong if it has a systematic offset.
A measure of the spread of individual values around the mean; it describes variability in the data.
SD divided by the square root of n; it describes the uncertainty in the estimate of the mean, and shrinks as n grows.
Technical replicates repeat measurement of the same sample; biological replicates are independent samples. Statistical inference about biology requires the latter.
Fitting a straight line by least squares; report slope and intercept with uncertainty and check residuals, not just R squared.
The probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis were true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true or the size of an effect.
A range of values computed so that, over repeated experiments, a stated percentage would contain the true parameter; more informative than a bare p-value.
Combining uncertainties from individual measurements into the uncertainty of a calculated result.

deeper.beginner: Repeat your measurement several times and calculate the mean. Report the spread with the standard deviation, and say how many independent samples there were (n). Plot data with error bars and state in the legend what they show. Keep units and sensible significant figures, and state the conclusion in plain words: what changed, by how much, and how sure you are.
deeper.intermediate: Before testing, plot the raw data, check for outliers and consider whether the assumptions of the test (roughly normal distribution, independence, similar variances) are reasonable. Use a two-sample t-test (or paired t-test for matched samples) for two groups, ANOVA with post hoc tests for several groups, and report effect size and confidence interval as well as p. For calibration, fit the line, read unknowns by interpolation and avoid extrapolating outside the standards. In reports, use a figure for patterns and a table for exact values, number and caption each so that it can be understood alone, and state clearly which results are your own and which come from sources. Never delete data without a stated reason.
deeper.advanced: Replicates define the experimental unit: measuring ten wells from one culture gives one biological replicate, and treating them as ten inflates significance (pseudoreplication). SEM bars reflect only sample size and spread, and overlap of SEM bars is a poor guide to significance, whereas 95 percent confidence intervals are easier to interpret; the choice must be declared. Non-linear least squares (for example fitting Michaelis-Menten data) gives parameter estimates with confidence intervals and should be preferred to linearisation, with residuals checked for pattern. Multiple testing inflates false positives and needs correction. Reproducibility is improved by pre-specifying the analysis, keeping raw data and scripts (R, Python) rather than relying on manual spreadsheet edits, and reporting methods fully; large surveys of researchers find that a majority have failed to reproduce another group's experiment, which is why this matters.

commonMistakes: Reporting SEM in a figure without saying so, or choosing SEM because the bars look smaller.
Treating technical replicates as independent samples in a statistical test.
Fitting a straight line to curved data and quoting R squared as proof that the model is right.
Quoting results to more significant figures than the measurement justifies, or rounding intermediate values during calculation.
